catatanpemred patriot bond gotong royong: editorial note patriot bond cooperation in the new face of nationalism at the end of August a new term emerged in our public space patriot bond a simple name but full of meaning andantara, the newly established sovereign wealth fund through government regulation no. of the year announced it will issue this bond in the upcoming October the targeted amount is quite large Rp50 trillion divided into two series with five- and seven-year tenors but larger than that number is its symbolism a call for capital owners to participate in funding the nation's future even with returns far below the market legally patriot bond is clearly different from government bonds it is not a fiscal instrument backed by the state budget but a corporate bond issued by andantara and supervised by the Financial Services Authority the state does not provide explicit guarantees but the government’s reputation is certainly at stake at this point andantara is trying a new way to build a fiscal bridge without increasing the state budget burden If we look back at history, this is not the first time the republic has raised funds under the banner of patriotism. Just a year after independence, the government issued a national loan based on the law, and the people, who were living in a wartime situation, bought bonds to finance the young republic. The difference is that back then the target was the general public; now, what is asked to participate collectively is the class of large capital owners. The spirit is the same, nationalism interpreted in the form of financial contracts. The reason for its launch is also not hard to understand: our fiscal space is getting tighter, the deficit is limited by law, while investment needs for renewable energy, waste management, to job creation continue to grow. Japan and the United States have done something similar, issuing patriotic bonds to mobilize citizen participation like during a crisis. Now it is Indonesia's turn to try its own way. Voices of support come from all corners, Rosan Roeslani, CEO of andantara as well as minister. The head of BKPM acknowledged that the major tycoons have already shown interest. 'Yes, they are interested, all of them want to participate,' he said while mentioning that the Barito Group and Djarum Group are among those ready to join. Pandu Patria Sjahrir, Chief Investment Officer (CIO) of Andantara who is also a commissioner of the Indonesia Stock Exchange, emphasized that the patriot bond is not coercion but an invitation for mutual cooperation, which is commonly practiced in many countries among conglomerates. Support was voiced by Prajogo Pangestu, founder and chairman of the Barito Pacific Group, who stated that development is the responsibility of all parties and the patriot bond provides an opportunity for the business world to contribute through good governance. Franky Oesman Widjaja, chairman and CEO of Sinar Mas Agribusiness & Food, as well as CEO of Golden Agri Resources Ltd, emphasized the multiple benefits: there is investment certainty as well as the acceleration of inclusive growth. Garibaldi Boy Thohir, president director of PT Adaro Energy Indonesia Tbk, spoke about the spirit of concrete mutual cooperation because of the funds. This will be used to fund a waste-to-energy project that is greatly needed by the community, of course, criticism has also arisen; some say the coupons are too low, almost like an obligatory charity rather than an investment instrument. Wijayanto Samirin, an economist at Paramadina University, reminds that there should not be an impression that the involvement of big entrepreneurs is merely due to political pressure. Doddy Ariefianto, an economist and lecturer at Binus University, emphasizes that the patriot bond must comply with capital market regulations; there must be a prospectus, transparency, and clear reporting to the OJK. At this point, however, what is needed is precisely transparency and strict governance, as reminded by Pandu Sjahrir. The key lies in a clear prospectus, routine audits, and open reporting. In this way, skepticism can be closed off and trust can grow. Ultimately, the patriot bond is not merely a fiscal instrument; it is a test of our togetherness. On paper, it is valued at Rp50 trillion, but behind that, it holds another value that is far greater, which is that Today's nationalism can find its face in the pages of bonds, that mutual cooperation does not stop at the rice barn or communal work, but can appear at the boardroom table and investment portfolio, and for entrepreneurs who choose to put their money in patriot bonds, it is not just a financial decision, it is a declaration of love for Indonesia. Eddy Prastyo, editor-in-chief of Suara Surabaya, media on patriotic bonds, collective courage.

pak budi bekerja sebagai supervisor oper: Mr. Budi works as an operational supervisor at a private company, is married, and has one child who is studying at a state university. A few years ago, his salary was Rp15 million gross per month, with income tax withheld of around Rp900 thousand. After he got a promotion, his salary increased to Rp22 million, and his monthly tax deduction also rose to almost Rp2 million. The problem is that the income increase also made his family be considered more capable financially. When his child entered a state university, Mr. Budi's family was again considered well-off, the tuition fee was categorized into a higher group, and educational aid and subsidies started to be reduced. Mr. Budi experienced an effective marginal burden, where each income increase does not fully translate into increased welfare because part of it is absorbed by higher taxes. Meanwhile, food prices rise, fuel becomes more expensive, mortgage payments continue, education costs increase, and the rupiah weakens. Mr. Budi’s planning from the beginning was based on salary surplus, savings, and asset investment. The problem is that the surplus keeps being eroded before it has a chance to materialize. Becoming wealthy statistically, Mr. Budi is already in the decile, but financially, he is not yet there—like his house is still being paid off in installments, his children are still in college, and losing a job for just a few months can still shake the family's finances. Formal groups like Mr. Budi are the easiest to tax because their income is recorded: when his salary increases, the tax increases; when his decile rises, the subsidy decreases; inflation and the weakening of the rupiah then erode the rest. Then Mr. Budi sees others who, after just a few years, already have a position or project access, big houses, land, expensive cars, and assets everywhere, while he has been working properly for almost ten years and is still counting installments. Thoughts begin to arise: 'I work properly for ten years, pay taxes, pay for my children's education, the subsidy is reduced, and I might not even be like those who do projects and earn interest; after a few years, they already have everything.' Here is where the issues of taxes, subsidies, inflation, and social mobility start to intersect with corruption. Of course, Mr. Budi does not automatically become a corruptor, but If the legal path to wealth is continually made longer and impossible while the rent-seeking path appears openly much shorter, the system is creating bad incentives, and corruption can no longer be read merely as an individual moral problem. When law-abiding people find it increasingly difficult to turn income into wealth, while rent-seeking and corruption offer much faster results, then it is the country's ecosystem that is making shortcuts seem increasingly rational.

According to him, deciles have the potential to become a justification for reducing assistance to the community amid the government's fiscal pressure. "If I look at Indonesia's current economic condition, it is not good at all and experiences a fiscal deficit every month. My analysis is that the ten-decile scenario was introduced due to limitations in social assistance and government subsidies," Subarsono said on Thursday. He assessed that through this system, the government is trying to narrow down the group of social assistance recipients using a new welfare category, even though people who are removed from the recipient list due to falling into certain deciles do not necessarily experience significant economic changes compared to the previous year. Therefore, the government is attempting to reduce the types of social assistance. or subsidies to the public by looking for justifying reasons that can still be debated, he said. As for the decile system, it divides society into ten groups based on household economic welfare. Problems arise when this classification is used as a basis to determine whether someone is still entitled to receive social assistance or not. According to Subarsono, this condition shows that the government needs to re-examine the validity of the indicators used to determine deciles. He questioned whether these categories can truly represent the real wealth and economic capacity of the community. It is appropriate for the public to question the validity of the measures used in these decile categories, he said.

pernyataan rektor ugm soal gaji dosen ra: The UGM rector's statement about the average lecturer salary being around million can actually be explained using the principles shown in the illustration below. This issue can perhaps be explained with the basic principles of statistics, namely measures of central tendency. For example, if it is true that there are lecturers who receive even above a million while the majority of lecturers mostly receive a million, mathematically the average can indeed approach a million. But the question is not whether the average is a million; a more important question is whether that number represents the condition of the majority of lecturers. This is where the role of the median becomes important. Many people consider the mean as the best way to describe the condition of a group, but that is not always the case. If the median salary happens to be around a million while the average is a million, then the number of a million does not represent the majority of lecturers. There is a bias caused by outliers. Simply put, the average lecturer salary is pushed up by a small number of very high salaries and that number becomes misleading if It is used to represent the majority, so the data is not necessarily false; what can be wrong is the choice of metrics because statistics is not just about counting numbers. Statistics is about representing reality. Can this be called data manipulation? I cannot conclude that far because I have not seen the data used. But one thing is clear: presenting statistics without explaining the data distribution can lead to misleading conclusions. What makes this case more interesting is that the statement was made by a rector. There should be an understanding that the average and median can tell very different realities because, in the end, the numbers can be correct, but the representation can be wrong. Data never lies; the person representing the data is the one who can manipulate it.

fakta dari sidang maka ini nunjukkin ada: The facts from the trial show that there is a legal vacuum. Lecturers are regulated under the Teacher and Lecturer Law, which is lex specialis, but their status as workers is not clearly affirmed in the labor law, which is lex generalis. The consequence is evident: private university lecturers are subjected to unilateral layoffs, and the labor office refuses to process it because it is considered not a regular employment relationship. In reality, the elements of wages, orders, and work—the three conditions of an employment relationship—are still fulfilled. Ironically, the basic salary is often below the minimum wage, even though the workload includes teaching, research, community service, and mentoring, often exceeding the weekly hours. This clearly contradicts the spirit of the constitutional articles on the right to a decent livelihood. Therefore, it must be affirmed that lecturers' basic salaries should be at least equivalent to the minimum wage, and their legal status should receive clear protection. The state cannot demand the quality of higher education while leaving its educators in a legal gray area.
fakta mengejutkan dari sidang maka banya: Shocking facts from the hearings show that many lecturers in Indonesia, even in public universities, are paid below the minimum wage, especially in the early years of their careers. In private universities, even more lecturers are paid below the minimum wage. The root of the problem is the ambiguous legal status of lecturers; it is regulated by the Law on Teachers and Lecturers but it is unclear whether they are also protected by labor law. As a result, many cases of lecturer termination are rejected by the labor office because they are considered not ordinary employment relationships. Ironically, the basic salary of lecturers is often below the minimum wage, even though their workload is not just teaching but also research, community service, and student guidance, which often exceeds weekly hours. Meanwhile, student tuition fees continue to rise without any guarantee that lecturers' salaries will increase. The state needs to ensure that the basic salary of lecturers is at least equal to the minimum wage and that their legal status is clearly protected by labor law. Education cannot progress if the lecturers themselves live below a decent standard of living.

iziiinn analisis konflik kepentingan pro: Let's analyze the conflict of interest in the new URI campus project. The gist is that the government's decision to create a new institution like the Republic of Indonesia University (URI) clearly seems vulnerable to conflicts of interest. To make it easier to understand, I'll break it down into these parts: the political interests of the authorities versus the public's needs. The fact is, the president created URI which is fully funded by the state budget, completely free. The target is to build the campus and focus on producing strategic leaders. The problem is, on the other hand, existing state universities like UI, UGM, ITB, etc., are still struggling with research funds, lecturer salaries, and lab facilities. Why it makes sense to call it a conflict of interest: officials choose to start a new project that's easier for building political image and legacy rather than fixing the old system that's already there. It's more controlled; the curriculum is easier, and it's also easier to produce people loyal to the regime. Militaristic style, close associates enter the campus. In fact, the URI governor is directly led by retired Air Marshal Donny Ermawan Taufanto, a former... The deputy defense minister is a typical pattern of the Prabowo era; important positions are placed by people from the military-defense circle. The problem is that a campus should be a neutral, autonomous, and fair place. Why does it make sense to say there is a conflict of interest if led by a former military person? The concern is that the academic vibe could become stiff like a military barrack, plus the potential for job patronage after graduation could increase, opening gaps for major projects and rent-seeking. The fact is, building a new campus from scratch, including dormitories and operations, requires a significant amount of state budget money. The problem is, here big physical projects often become an easy arena for dividing procurement tenders, from goods to consultants. Why does it make sense to say there is a conflict of interest if the person deciding we need a new campus is the same person who controls trillions in the budget? It’s a different story if the funds are used to upgrade an existing public university, where the monitoring system is already clearer. Bringing personal vision into state facilities, in fact, Prabowo has always been closely associated with education issues. nationality, for example, once held the National Education Foundation of UKRI Bandung, now making URI with a very similar concept. Why it makes sense to call it a conflict of interest, there is a thin line between personal family ambition regarding the concept of a national school and the extravagant use of state money to realize it. In conclusion, the government will definitely make excuses, claiming it is for the interest of the nation, but if seen from the perspective of conflict of interest, the pattern clearly creates a new toy that is easily controlled and safe for their political interests. They prefer to ignore fixing the old autonomous campus which is hard to manage, even though that is what the public really needs. Not directly accusing of corruption, but just from the structure, it is already apparent that it is flawed and full of self-interest.

ternyata isu gaji dosen ini bisa melahir: It turns out that the issue of lecturers' salaries can create drama not much different from the way the government responds to public problems when there are real complaints in the field, instead presenting average data that seems convincing as if everything is fine. One UGM lecturer, Nabiyla Risfa Izzati, an expert in labor law, once brought data and arguments to court stating that the basic salary of lecturers should at least be equivalent to the minimum wage as a safety net, because it is the only fixed component received from the first year. She also highlighted that the average income of national lecturers is still low, around IDR 3 million, with many earning below the minimum wage. Other testimonies from campus labor unions and non-ASN UGM lecturers also revealed the reality of income far from decent, with reports of cases at the level of hundreds of thousands of rupiah. However, just a few weeks later, UGM rector Ova Emilia presented in court in July that the average take-home pay of lecturers at the university reaching Rp20 million for lecturers, Rp25 million for assistant experts, Rp33 million for associate professors, Rp38 million for full professors, and Rp45 million for professors. Two data sets from the same institution, but the resulting picture is very different. On one side, it highlights vulnerability and inequality; on the other, it shows numbers that seem prosperous. I am surprised that the rector seems to be covering up this issue by presenting seemingly high average salary data. Why not present it as it is, complete with median distribution and differences between civil servant lecturers and non-civil servant lecturers, junior lecturers, or across faculties? This pattern reminds me of how the government often responds to teacher and lecturer welfare issues—emphasizing overall or average budget increases without breaking down who actually benefits and who is still left behind. Aggregate figures become a shield while disparities at the lower level remain ignored. By only showing high averages, an institution can appear to have successfully maintained lecturer welfare, whereas on average it is very easily skewed by a small group receiving structural allowances, large grants, or senior positions, while lecturers at lower levels, who actually need protection the most, remain in this vulnerable zone. This risks weakening the push for setting national minimum standards currently being tested, as if the problem only occurs in other campuses. If the data is truly complete and transparent, there should be nothing to fear. In fact, by revealing the full distribution, campuses can show where improvements have already been made and where work still remains. Presenting only the positive side actually makes the public and judges wonder whether this is an effort to maintain the image, protect the autonomy of the state university, or if there is indeed inequality that is more comfortable hiding behind average figures. The issue of lecturer salaries should be a space for honesty, not a forum for claiming data from one another, because what is at stake is not only the reputation of one campus but the future quality. higher education and the overall dignity of the lecturer profession

pada selasa mahkamah konstitusi maka men: On Tuesday, the Constitutional Court held a continued session to review Law No. [year] concerning teachers and lecturers. This session combined two case petitions, No. PUU XXIII and PUU XXIV, submitted by lecturers and campus labor unions demanding rights to fair and just income, welfare, and allowances. The agenda of the session was to hear statements from five state universities with legal entity status (PTN BH) regarding how they manage lecturer income components at their respective campuses. Explanations: Hasanuddin University (UNHAS) implements the same standard salary and basic rights, or equates them, between permanent non-civil servant lecturers and lecturers with civil servant status (PNS). Income components include basic salary, fixed allowances, family allowances, and social security. Airlangga University (UNAIR) divides income components into fixed income (basic salary, additional functional allowances, and professional allowances for certified lecturers) and variable income (incentives). Regarding performance achievements, basic salary is not the only source of income at UNAIR. Gadjah Mada University (UGM) uses three financial compensation systems: P1 pay per person in the form of basic salary and attached allowances; P2 payment based on position, risk, and pay for performance, incentives based on academic and research performance, etc. Universitas Indonesia (UI), like UGM, also measures welfare through the components of pay per person, pay for position, and pay for performance. di dunia psikologi dan sosiologi ini ser: In the world of psychology and sociology, this is often called crab mentality or fear of changing the status quo. The biased mindset of professors who are overly critical of this struggle for rights is actually a residue of upbringing and childhood education that may not have been resolved. For example, the 'sweet child syndrome' or blind obedience in many traditional preschools: children considered good and high-achieving are those who sit quietly, obey, don’t ask many questions, and do not protest. Children who demand a lot or protest are labeled fussy or naughty. This carries on into adulthood; they feel that a good professor is one who passively accepts whatever affection and salary is given, while protest is considered naughty and disruptive to order. The zero-sum game mentality of scarcity—have you ever heard a teacher say, 'Whoever sits the neatest can go home first'? This instills a false sense of competition in children; they are taught that rewards, praise, and benefits are limited and given by the authority of the teacher. If another friend receives them, it means I am threatened with not getting any. As adults, they feel that supporting colleagues who are struggling will threaten their secure position in the eyes of their superiors. The ministry campus looks for validation upward, not sideways, with little solidarity. Our early education system often does not emphasize equal collaboration. Children are busier seeking a gold star or praise from their teachers rather than building solidarity with their peers. Cynical lecturers may have a psychological drive to appear as the most loyal and straightforward employee in the eyes of the system, hoping that loyalty will bring rewards. Extreme conflict avoidance: children are often taught to just give in and not fight, without being taught how to handle conflict healthily and fight for their rights. As a result, when a colleague provokes conflict with the system for the common good, they feel anxious, disturbed, and end up attacking the colleague who is actually bringing the message.

menarik sekali mencermati keriuhan perde: It's really interesting to observe the uproar over the recent debates about lecturers' welfare, but it feels like we still enjoy arguing on the surface—very noisy and chaotic—but our focus only reaches up to the basic salary. Let's open up a bit of academic reflection, complete with numerical comparisons to make it a bit scientific. As a civil servant lecturer with many years of service, I have a basic salary in the range of millions. Now, if we look at the honorable constitutional judges, their basic salary is also in the range of millions at the base figure. Wow, very similar, right? It feels very equal and fair. However, here lies the beauty of our wage structure, which determines our fate at the end of the month—not the base figure, but the supporting variable, namely the position allowance. Let us appreciate the resilience of the historical monument of the lecturers' position allowance, which has been set since the year and has very consistently never changed to this day. Truly impressive, our allowance has proven resistant to the pace of inflation for almost two decades as an assistant expert. rp375 per lecturer, rp700 for head lecturer, rp900 for professor, rp1. Meanwhile, just for an objective comparison, the honorable judges' position allowance ranges from millions to millions of rupiah, which is certainly an extraordinary appreciation. The critical point is, why was our struggle yesterday only busy arguing over basic salaries? If we are honest and realistic, what determines whether the household runs smoothly or not is a decent take-home pay (THP), not just the basic components. And remember, this circle of struggle does not only belong to civil servant lecturers but also our colleagues who are permanent lecturers in foundations or PTNBH, whose fate is often more challenging than large private university lecturers or small private university lecturers, who are barely getting by. In court, the lecturers' version from SPK and FKDSI claimed they were paid below the regional minimum wage, some with a basic salary of Rp 1 million, and there were even payslips of Rp 340 thousand per month. secara konsep tunjangan lebih mudah diub: Conceptually, allowances are easier to change than the basic salary. The basic salary is the foundation, and if it is increased significantly, the burden falls on the state budget (APBN/APBD) because its effects spread to many other components such as pensions, holiday allowances, salaries, contributions, and the overall structure of employee expenditure at the national level. That is why the government feels more comfortable keeping the basic salary relatively small and then increasing take-home pay through allowances. If the basic salary has a larger share or everything is turned into a single salary, the government would find it very difficult to reduce it because the salary is considered a permanent right; once increased, it is almost impossible to decrease. Meanwhile, allowances are more flexible; although they still burden the state budget (APBN/APBD), they can be differentiated based on position, agency, region, performance, or budget capacity.

semua tentu setuju profesi apapun mening: Everyone would certainly agree that any profession earns more income, the question is how. In state universities, there are two types of lecturers: civil servant lecturers and non-civil servant lecturers. Civil servant lecturers have a basic salary tied to their rank, not to their job type. So a civil servant who works as a teacher, a public health center doctor, or a heart specialist lecturer will have the same basic salary as long as their rank is the same. It is not possible, for example, to increase the basic salary of one profession while ignoring another profession with the same rank and years of service; philosophically, no civil servant profession is more important than another. Non-civil servant lecturers are recruited by the university itself and their salary is independently managed by the university that recruits them. Their situation is similar to honorary teachers because these lecturers are not civil servants. The salary of non-civil servant lecturers does not come from the state budget. The state university that recruits non-civil servant lecturers pays their salary from the university's own income, such as student tuition fees, in accordance with the Public University Law, and its use is managed independently by the university. The campus, how much the salary of non-civil servant lecturers depends on the financial capability of the recruiting campus. Logically, if the campus has to raise the salary, the most likely way is by increasing the income of the state university; one way the income is sourced is from UKT and initial fees.

sedang ramai soal kesaksian dosen unair: It's been busy regarding the testimony of a UNAIR lecturer at the court, to the point where there are threads making posts as if UNAIR objects to their testimony and will contest it. I checked with friends at UNAIR, and no one is going to contest the testimony. It's just that the former rector of UNAIR explained on social media the income received by new non-civil servant lecturers at UNAIR with qualifications like those shown in Cenuk's video. Radian also sent an official release detailing the monthly income of permanent non-civil servant lecturers, which is well above the Surabaya minimum wage. That's just UNAIR's response, which I think is reasonable. For balance, I support the campus workers' union in taking legal action to the court concerning the articles in the law on teachers and lecturers regarding lecturer salaries, where there is no guarantee of a proper and certain minimum wage, unlike the wage guarantees for labor with the minimum wage. However, if I observe Cenuk's video testimony and the real facts and data as a new non-civil servant lecturer at UNAIR, I think it's somewhat inaccurate. I actually think he is not one of those affected by the uncertainty in the article of the law that is tied to his status as a lecturer at Unair because the salary he receives every month, which is certain and fixed from Unair, is actually above the Surabaya minimum wage, excluding allowances or other additional payments as a researcher, even when he just started that year. Besides, the impression that arises from that testimony is as if he had been working at Unair for over a decade when in fact he hadn't, because he only joined Unair that year. It is the same as a worker moving to a new position at a new place, which is not a continuation of the old place; it depends on the position that is opened and applied for, and that is still called a new employee or a new lecturer at Unair. That’s all I see, miss. It’s as if Unair is being judged in public by that testimony, as if it gives an unacceptable salary to a doctor who has worked for over ten years. Basically, the lawsuit concerns the minimum salary for lecturers, which has been inconsistent, uncertain, and without guarantee all this time. Just as workers whose wages are guaranteed must follow the minimum wage (UMR) set by the regional government, in the minimal wage scheme, it is certain that wages cannot be given below that amount. The minimum wage is a combination of base salary and fixed allowances, where the minimum base salary is part of the total combination of base salary and fixed allowances. Now, the problem in the article is that the allowance components for lecturers are all variable, not fixed, with only the base salary being fixed, while the allowances are based on various measures that are not the same, for example, performance allowance, child allowance, Serdos allowance, etc. Imagine, for instance, a single lecturer who is not yet Serdos and just started teaching—what would their monthly wage be? It would only be the base salary, which is guaranteed according to the law, plus maybe a meal allowance. Hence, many lecturers are paid below the city or district UMR. This is unfair, and this is what is being contested, especially as the article locks the wage amount, tying it to agreements in employment contracts. Truly, the fate of lecturers is included in this. Teachers include the situation of my cousin who became a lecturer, which was conveyed by Cenuk, and actually represents many lecturers whose monthly wages are below the minimum wage, and this is based on the current teacher and lecturer law which is legally binding and cannot be contested, unlike workers who can sue a company if they are paid below the minimum wage. So the real issue is, what is the definition of minimum wage for lecturers? If the demands of the parties are accepted, then the basic salary of lecturers would be the minimum reference, the same as the city/regency minimum wage, while lecturers' allowances, because they are variable and uncertain, cannot be included as a component in determining fixed wages. That's roughly it. Hopefully, the judicial review carried out by SPK will be approved by the judge, which will of course also impact the payment of teachers since government funds exist, right? How can MBak and Kdmp provide hundreds of trillions for the allocation of minimum lecturer wages? It certainly cannot be allocated for private universities or private schools. di depan ribuan guru besar prabowo ingat: In front of thousands of professors, Prabowo reminds the importance of cooperation among elites for the nation's revival. Jakarta – Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto reminded of the importance of unity, solidarity, and cooperation among the nation's elites as key for Indonesia to achieve progress and prosperity. This was conveyed by Prabowo during the opening of the Indonesian Science, Technology, and Industry Convention (KSTI) as well as a national seminar with rectors and lecturers from state universities (PTN) and private universities (PTS) across Indonesia, themed 'Strategies for Economic Independence and Indonesia's Prosperity,' at the Jakarta Convention Center, Jakarta, on Friday. In front of thousands of professors, scientists, and academics from various universities, Prabowo said that each individual may have different backgrounds, whether in terms of ethnicity, religion, profession, experience, expertise, or perspectives. However, amid these various differences, he reminded of the importance of finding common points. According to him, this is necessary in order to All elements of the nation can work together to achieve a common goal, namely the advancement of the nation and the optimization of Indonesia's potential. Nations whose elites can cooperate are nations that rise, while nations whose elites can never cooperate cannot reach their potential, Prabowo stated clearly. He said that this view stems from lessons about world history. According to him, history shows that nations whose elites remain trapped in division will find it difficult to achieve progress. In this regard, he exemplified several prolonged conflicts in various parts of the world, such as in Ukraine, Lebanon, and the Arab Gulf region, where one of the causes is the failure of the elites in each area to build cooperation. 'From what I have learned from thousands of years of history, nations whose elites can cooperate succeed, while nations whose elites can never cooperate cannot reach their potential. Once a year, Indonesia carries out the largest statistical event besides the population census: the economic census, and this year it's the turn of the 2026 economic census, which is in the spotlight. This is no small matter; it is a state project that touches almost every corner of business activity in Indonesia. The economic census is one of the three major national censuses conducted periodically by BPS, along with the population census and the agricultural census. Its main purpose is to obtain basic data on the national economic structure as a foundation for planning and evaluating development in the economic sector. The data collection process is carried out by BPS based on the mandate of Law Number [year] on Statistics, and the 2026 economic census is the fifth economic census conducted by BPS. With a budget of IDR 1 trillion, BPS emphasized that the IDR 1 trillion budget is allocated to ensure the smooth running of data collection, which is scheduled to take place from May to July. BPS's principal secretary Zulkipli stated that the current budget support is in a stable condition even though there are efficiency measures because this is mandated by the law; the economic census must be carried out with a total budget of around IDR 1 trillion in 2026, which will capture all economic activities in provinces and regencies/cities with the exception of the agricultural sector, government administration, and household activities for own consumption. The target includes more than one million business units across Indonesia. In 2026, it will be implemented in two stages: the first phase in May through the CAWI (Computer Assisted Web Interviewing) method for large businesses that have email, while the second phase runs from May to July using the CAPI (Computer Assisted Personal Interview) method targeting micro, small, and medium enterprises as well as large businesses that do not yet have email. BPS needs field officers for the implementation of the economic census. The Deputy Head of BPS RI, Sonny Harry Budiutomo Harmadi, stated that we need thousands of field officers, who can be students, lecturers, or academicians. Joining because this is labor-intensive across Indonesia, how much is the salary of payment system officers based on work volume rather than a fixed monthly salary for the field enumerator (PCL) position? Officers are responsible for conducting direct interviews with business actors, with an estimated honorarium of around IDR 3 million to IDR 4 million per month, while field supervisors (PML), who verify digital questionnaires, are estimated to receive an honorarium of around IDR 4 million to IDR 5 million per month. The officers' work period is about three months, namely June to August. The status as statistical partners is contract workers for the activity, not permanent employees, civil servants, or government contract employees (PPPK). The estimated cost breakdown is IDR 1 trillion, with no official details by position published. However, based on the pattern of large BPS censuses, the largest costs are estimated to be distributed to the following positions: the average officer honorarium per month is around IDR 3 million, and for three months, it is estimated to absorb about IDR 1 trillion. This figure exceeds the total budget, meaning that most officers receive more than one contract. short or honorarium below average other cost items include procurement and rental of digital devices, training and technical guidance for thousands of officers nationwide, field operational costs, transportation, accommodation in remote areas, technology infrastructure and national data servers, publicity campaigns and outreach to millions of business actors, as well as cross-ministry and agency coordination. The big question: with a budget of Rp1 trillion to register more than a million business units in regencies and cities, the cost per business unit is only around Rp30, cheaper than a cup of coffee in a mall. This makes Indonesian teachers' salaries the lowest in Southeast Asia. Another fact is that quite a number of teachers are even paid below the regional minimum wage. The Teachers and Education Association (P2G) recorded that there are still teachers who are paid only hundreds of thousands of rupiah per month. Why are teachers’ salaries still low? How is the budget allocation governance managed? Has there been any solution-oriented scheme in education so far to ensure the welfare of educators? How is the practice in other countries? In the public space of KBR, we will discuss it together with the head of research and development of the Education and Teachers Association P2G, Feriyansyah, and education observer from UIN Jakarta, Jejen Musfah, livestreaming on KBR Media YouTube. banyak masyarakat yang terjebak pada jud: Many people get trapped by headlines without understanding the substance, for example, when Finance Minister Sri Mulyani revealed that the welfare budget for ASN and non-ASN teachers reached Rp81 trillion, an increase of Rp16 trillion in November, many immediately reacted, whereas her statement was only a reflective question: should teacher welfare fully depend on state finances, or is there a role for public participation? Unfortunately, when it enters the media realm, this question is often twisted into a narrative far from the context. The question about public participation is actually relevant, but reality on the ground shows contradictions in public attitudes. Take, for example, the Eid moment when a video of a student giving a simple gift, like instant noodles or cooking oil, to their teacher went viral on social media. The value of the gifts was insignificant, ranging from Rp5 to Rp10 per student, and some as little as Rp2. The response of netizens, instead of appreciation, many Instead, they insult the teacher, accusing him of exploiting students by asking for donations. On the other hand, when a school raises tuition fees to improve the welfare of the teachers, parents collectively protest, arguing that the school is considered to already receive government assistance, so the tuition increase is regarded as a capitalist action. In fact, government assistance is often not enough to cover the operational needs of the school, let alone the welfare of non-civil servant teachers who are often neglected. So what about other sources of funding, such as taxes, which should be the backbone of public funding but are only paid by a small portion of society? When the government relies on natural resources to increase revenue, protests arise accusing environmental destruction. If the government encourages investment by building factories, local residents often take advantage of the situation to extort investors through community organizations. When enforcement is carried out, large-scale demonstrations occur. erupting with the narrative that the government is silencing the common people, ironically if foreign investors come in, the accusation that the country is sold rings out. So what exactly are the hopes of the people? It is hard not to see a pattern where the government is always the party blamed for any policy. Questions about public participation in the welfare of teachers and lecturers are not about assigning blame but rather an invitation to take responsibility together. However, when every step is obstructed by contradictory attitudes, solutions become increasingly difficult to formulate. Society needs to reflect: if it is not only the government that must take action, then what is our role in supporting better education?

In accordance with the constitutional mandate, the government has allocated an education budget of IDR 724 trillion or its equivalent from the state budget for this fiscal year. The state budget is also allocated for LPDP scholarships, digitalization of learning, professional teacher allowances (TPG) for non-civil servant teachers for 200 thousand teachers, certification for 225 thousand teachers, the construction and rehabilitation of 20 thousand schools, as well as the Free Nutritious Meal Program (MBak). In addition, Sri Mulyani also explained that the budget Education is divided into three main clusters. The first cluster is the budget allocated for the benefit of students up to university students. memenuhi undangan article focus group di: attending the invitation to an article focus group discussion (FGD) on the national education system bill (RUU Sisdiknas) with the topic of compulsory education several points of fulfilling compulsory education expansion of compulsory education years implications for private schools the expansion of compulsory education from a certain number of years including pre-institution to upper secondary is a progressive step to increase access to education however, private schools, especially community-based ones like Muhammadiyah, face financial and operational challenges private schools serve the majority of Indonesian students with limited resources compared to public schools without a clear funding mechanism, the financial burden can hinder the implementation of the role of private schools private schools, especially the Muhammadiyah network, play a key role in fulfilling the mandate of compulsory education, particularly in areas less accessible to public schools the national education law article states that the responsibility for compulsory education is shared between the government, local governments, and the community, with private schools as an important component however, their contributions are often underrecognized in compulsory education financing policies. The National Education System Law (UU Sisdiknas) does not clearly regulate government funding for private schools. Private schools serving low-income communities struggle to provide free education without financial support. The expansion of compulsory education increases operational costs such as teacher salaries and facilities, which can force schools to charge fees, contrary to the goal of free education. Regional disparities and decentralization present challenges. Private schools in remote areas where Muhammadiyah operates face uneven support due to decentralization. The National Education System Law needs to address disparities in the capacity of local governments to support private schools in underdeveloped regions. Technological and pedagogical innovation: revisions to the National Education System Law should support innovations such as artificial intelligence (AI), differentiated learning, and flexible educational pathways. Muhammadiyah has integrated technology despite limitations. Private schools need support to meet the demands of 21st-century education for inclusivity and non-discrimination. Muhammadiyah is committed to inclusive education, serving students from diverse backgrounds. The revision of the National Education System Law must ensure access to education for marginalized communities without discriminatory barriers. The harmonization of education laws and overlapping regulations between the National Education System Law and other laws, for example, the Teachers and Lecturers Law and the Pesantren Law, creates administrative burdens for private schools. A cohesive legal framework is needed to support private schools, including those based on religion. Community participation, the Muhammadiyah community-based education model, involves local stakeholders in school governance. The revision of the National Education System Law must formalize this model to enhance accountability and the relevance of education.

This was stated by Coordinating Minister AHY after delivering a public lecture at the regular education at the Army Staff and Command School (SESKOAD) in Bandung, West Java on Monday. Coordinating Minister AHY said the government will continue to build cross-ministerial and institutional cooperation to make Indonesia more advanced. This effort is expected to strengthen national resilience in facing global challenges and international competition. 'We hope the government continues to build synergy and collaboration with various elements of the nation. Of course, in my capacity as Coordinating Minister for Infrastructure and Regional Development, this becomes one of the priorities,' said Coordinating Minister AHY during the opportunity of delivering the public lecture. Coordinating Minister AHY discussed the importance of infrastructure development that is not only oriented towards economic growth and public welfare but also has a direct impact on the country's defense, according to him, this strengthens the relevance of the role of the Indonesian National Armed Forces, especially the Army, as an integral part of maintaining national stability. Vital infrastructure is often a benchmark for a nation's progress. Threats to critical infrastructure, including those related to the economy, food, water, energy, and tourism, can affect national stability. Therefore, synergy between infrastructure development and national defense becomes very important, he explained further. Coordinating Minister AHY emphasized that threats to national infrastructure not only affect the economy but also the safety and lives of the community, nation, and state. Hence, strong defense and a reliable TNI are required to protect national vital infrastructure. Conversely, the government also committed to supporting the Indonesian National Armed Forces (TNI) to be increasingly prepared as a national defense tool, supported by adequate military infrastructure including strengthening the connectivity and transportation sectors for military logistics and defense equipment to advance further in the future, he added. This public lecture at the regular education at SESKOAD was also attended by the SESKOAD commander, Major General TNI Edwin Adrian Sumantha, the main officials of SESKOAD, department heads, lecturer representatives, and SESKOAD staff and students in the regular class of SESKOAD in the year of MENKO AHY, accompanied by special staff Agust Jovan Latuconsina, I Made Rai Edi Astawa, and Sigit Raditya from Kemenkoinfra and Kemenko Infrastruktur, MENKOAHY infrastructure for all.

In this meeting, HIMPAUDI conveyed various strategic issues faced by non-formal early childhood educators, including the imbalance in professional recognition and their welfare. HIMPAUDI General Chairperson Betti Nuraini emphasized that until now, non-formal early childhood teachers have not received recognition as teachers as stipulated in Law Number [year] concerning teachers and lecturers. The majority of non-formal early childhood teachers still face welfare challenges with an average salary below IDR 250 per month. This is worsened by minimal legal protection and limited access to the teacher professional education program (PPG) for non-formal early childhood teachers. In response to the presentation Gamal appreciated the dedication of non-formal early childhood educators in educating the nation's generation. 'We highly appreciate the sincerity and dedication of colleagues in supporting education in Indonesia; however, sincerity and dedication do not mean being contrary to welfare,' said Gamal, who is also an expert council member of Himpaudi. As a strategic step, Gamal encouraged Himpaudi to continuously oversee this issue in the DPR and related ministries. Meanwhile, for KNB scholarships as well as lecturers and education personnel, he continued, the budget efficiency was a certain percentage of the initial ceiling, amounting to IDR 85 billion each. and Rp236 billion of the same budget component also includes provisions related to employee salaries and allowances as well as non-civil servant lecturer allowances. BMKG head Dwikorita Karnawati emphasized that innovation, collaboration, and discipline are the three main pillars in the transformation of the Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics College (STMKG). This effort is a strategic step to realize Golden Indonesia while also addressing global challenges such as climate change, geo-hydrometeorological disasters, and the demands for accelerated technological innovation. STMKG is not merely an educational institution but the foundation of civilization. Our nation needs a generation capable of managing data, turning it into information for the sake of human safety and welfare, and then advancing it to the level of knowledge and wisdom. From here, relevant and meaningful solutions can emerge, said Dwikorita in the STMKG transformation workshop towards Golden Indonesia in Tangerang on Thursday. According to her, the ability to observe Understanding, analyzing, processing, and utilizing data effectively is a fundamental skill that must be possessed in this era of information and technological advancement. Data that is processed quickly, accurately, and precisely becomes meaningful information and knowledge that can serve as a foundation for strategic decision-making with wide-reaching impacts. Without deep understanding of data, the great potential contained within it will only be overlooked. Data is like a golden key; if we cannot process it, we will only be overwhelmed by a flood of information. Therefore, STMKG must ensure that its students, the cadets, are not only able to collect and process data into important, easily understood information, but are also able to apply, utilize, and disseminate this information to save and improve the welfare of society, as well as support government policies. In addition, Dwikorita emphasized that cross-disciplinary collaboration within STMKG or with Various external parties are key to creating more innovative and precise solutions. It encourages cadet students and lecturers from various study programs to collaborate under a single cross-disciplinary or cross-study program research umbrella so that every point of view or problem-solving approach can contribute to addressing complex challenges. According to him, this collaboration not only strengthens STMKG internally but also prepares it to compete at the national and global levels. Collaboration is not just about working together, but also about managing differences into a comprehensive and precise solution. Create a research umbrella that involves lecturers and students across study programs and institutions; in this way, we can develop innovations and solve problems accurately and effectively. In addition, he added, international collaboration must also be a priority to make STMKG relevant not only at the national level. but also acknowledged its role and reputation globally. She mentioned that cooperation with international institutions, student exchange programs, and joint research are concrete steps towards this goal. Dwikorita also reminded that innovation without being accompanied by morality and wisdom can become a serious threat that endangers. Because the ability to predict and analyze climate data can help anticipate this problem, said Stella. Stella emphasized the importance of research and data analysis in the transformation of STMKG. STMKG must strengthen research based on local and national issues. BMKG data, which is rich in potential, can be utilized for problem-based learning. This will make STMKG graduates more prepared to face real challenges in the field. 'We need a generation capable of solving the nation's problems with a scientific and innovative approach. This transformation is not a choice but a necessity. With collaboration, innovation, and discipline, STMKG will become a center of excellence that is not only relevant at the national level but also recognized globally, he concluded. siaran pers dari aliansi dosen asn kemen: press release from the ASN lecturers alliance of Kemendiktisaintek throughout Indonesia, ADAXSI, January 2025 ADAXSI urges the government to immediately pay the performance allowance for ASN lecturers of Kemdiktisaintek for the year in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations, promoting justice for all ASN lecturers of Kemdiktisaintek Jakarta January performance allowance is a right that has been mandated since the year in Law No. of the year, Article on state civil apparatus, however, the right to performance allowance has never been felt by ASN lecturers of Kemdiktisaintek before and after the ASN law was enacted, while ASN lecturers in other ministries have received performance allowances since the year for the year, the right to performance allowance for ASN lecturers was excluded, and for the year the right that has been clearly regulated in the technical implementation of the payment of Permendikbud No. of the year, it was still not paid. The ASN lecturers alliance of Kemdiktisaintek throughout Indonesia, ADAXSI, fully supports the efforts of the Kemdiktisaintek legal team in drafting a new Presidential Regulation (Perpres) related to the performance allowance (tukin) for Employees within the Ministry of Higher Education, Research, and Technology (Kemdiktisaintek) state that this new presidential regulation must remove the exemption clauses that have so far hindered the provision of performance allowances (tukin) to lecturers in state universities (PTN) with public service agency (BLU) status and legal entity (BH) status, so that tukin can be given to PTN lecturers in BLU and BH work units, as well as Kemdiktisaintek civil servant lecturers seconded to private universities (PTS DPK) without any exceptions. Why tukin needs to be regulated fairly, Adaksi emphasizes that the equitable provision of tukin to all Kemdiktisaintek civil servant lecturers is an important step in creating fairness in the higher education environment. Some of the main considerations underlying the importance of this new presidential regulation include the long process of providing remuneration in BLU PTNs; many BLU PTNs require up to years to be able to provide remuneration to lecturers and educational staff.
